passages.t: A morning plea, and the God who hates evil
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster, to be accompanied by flutes. A Psalm of David” (verse 1).

The man begins by asking God to listen: “Give ear to my words, O LORD; consider my groaning” (verse 1). He calls God “my King and my God” (verse 2). And he prays at dawn: “In the morning, O LORD, You hear my voice; at daybreak I lay my plea before You and wait in expectation” (verse 3).

Then he says why he dares to come. God is holy. “For You are not a God who delights in wickedness; no evil can dwell with You” (verse 4). “The boastful cannot stand in Your presence; You hate all workers of iniquity” (verse 5). “You destroy those who tell lies” (verse 6).

Then a strong ‘But I’: “But I will enter Your house by the abundance of Your loving devotion; in reverence I will bow down toward Your holy temple” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Morning mattered in Israel's worship. A lamb was offered on the altar every morning and another at twilight (Exodus 29:38-39). Morning was a time to bring a request and then watch for God's answer.

‘I lay my plea before You’ uses a Hebrew verb for setting things out in order. It is used of arranging wood on an altar and of laying out a case in court. The man sets his prayer before God and then waits, like a watchman looking for the dawn.

‘Dwell’ in verse 4 can mean to stay as a guest. Evil cannot be God's guest.

‘Workers of iniquity’ means people who make a practice of doing wrong. Verse 6 names them more sharply: liars, people of ‘bloodshed and deceit’.

Verse 7 explains how the man himself can come in. Not because he is good enough, but “by the abundance of Your loving devotion”. ‘Loving devotion’ is the Hebrew hesed, God's faithful, promised love. He bows toward the temple, the way Israel prayed toward God's house even from far away. Daniel did this in Babylon, with his windows open toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10).

The heading links the psalm to David, but Solomon built the temple after David died. Readers answer this in two ways. Some think the psalm, or its final wording, comes from the time of the temple. Others point out that the same Hebrew words for ‘house’ and ‘temple’ were used of the earlier sanctuary, the tent where the ark was kept.
passages.later:
Solomon asked God to hear every prayer prayed “toward this place” (1 Kings 8:29-30).

Proverbs also speaks of what God hates: “six things that the LORD hates, seven that are detestable to Him”, among them “a lying tongue” and “hands that shed innocent blood” (Proverbs 6:16-17).

Yet God says through Ezekiel, “Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?” (Ezekiel 18:23). And Paul writes, “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

Revelation's picture of God's city echoes verse 4: “nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who practices an abomination or a lie” (Revelation 21:27).
passages.hard:
‘You hate all workers of iniquity.’ Doesn't God love everyone? This verse is strong, and it should not be softened. Christians hold it together with God's love in a few ways.

Some point to how Hebrew speaks. ‘Hate’ in the Bible often means firm rejection, a refusal to accept, more than a burst of feeling. On this reading the verse says God will not welcome evil into his presence or treat it as harmless.

Some distinguish two things in God's stance toward a person: his settled opposition to someone who keeps on doing evil, and his love for that same person as someone he made, whom he calls to turn and live (Ezekiel 18:23). Ezekiel and Paul (Romans 5:8) show that love reaching out to people while they are still his enemies.

Some stress the setting. Psalm 5 is a prayer from someone being wronged. It speaks like a plea in court, where the question is God's verdict on what has been done.

On any of these readings the psalm refuses a God who shrugs at lies and violence. For people who have been lied about or hurt, that is good news. And verse 7 keeps the psalmist humble: he enters only by God's mercy, as every worshipper does.
passages.asks:
Start tomorrow the way this psalm starts: early, before the day fills up. Set out your requests before God in order, and then watch, expecting him to answer.

And remember how the man got in the door: not by his goodness but by God's loving devotion. That is the only door anyone has.

passages.t: ‘Lead me’, and refuge for all who love God's name
passages.happening:
The man asks for guidance: “Lead me, O LORD, in Your righteousness because of my enemies; make straight Your way before me” (verse 8).

He describes his enemies by their words: “not a word they speak can be trusted; destruction lies within them. Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit” (verse 9). He asks God to judge them: “Declare them guilty, O God; let them fall by their own devices” (verse 10).

Then he turns to everyone who trusts God. “But let all who take refuge in You rejoice; let them ever shout for joy” (verse 11). He ends, “For surely You, O LORD, bless the righteous; You surround them with the shield of Your favor” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
‘Make straight Your way’ is a picture from travel. A straight, level path is easy to walk and hard to get lost on. The man asks God to make the right road plain while enemies watch for him to stumble.

‘Their throats are open graves’ is a vivid picture. An open grave smells of death. Out of these mouths come words that kill: lies, slander, plots.

‘Declare them guilty’ is the language of a law court. The man does not ask to punish them himself. He asks the judge to give the verdict. ‘Let them fall by their own devices’ means let their own schemes trip them up.

‘Refuge’ is a place to run to for safety. In verse 12 God's favour is a shield that surrounds the righteous on every side.

‘The righteous’ in the Psalms does not mean people who never sin. It means those who belong to God, trust him and seek his ways.
passages.later:
Paul quotes verse 9 in his long list of what sin does to every human being: “Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit” (Romans 3:13). For Paul these words describe not only the psalmist's enemies but all people without God, Jew and Gentile alike, himself included: “There is no one righteous, not even one” (Romans 3:10).

James warns that the tongue “is a fire” (James 3:6).

The ending, refuge and shield, runs right through the Psalms and returns in Psalm 91 and in many others.
passages.asks:
Paul takes the words this psalm says about enemies and says them about everyone, himself included. Before you pray against those who lie about you, ask where your own words have done harm.

Then pray verse 8: ‘Lead me.’ Ask God to make the right road plain in the place where you are most tempted to answer lies with lies.
